chunks.heading: Agronomy: the spray table and where it comes from
chunks.text: Status: researched on 20 October 2026 by the build team from published sources. Not yet reviewed by an agronomist. A named plant pathologist (ICAR-NRCP Solapur, MPKV Rahuri or the KVK) must review this table before any field use or public advice. The app never generates a product or a dose; it only shows what is in web/src/lib/sim/rules.ts, and that file follows this document.

chunks.heading: The table
chunks.text:
| Use in the app | Product | Dose | Interval | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Curative: after a scan confirms blight on the plot | Copper hydroxide 77% WP | 2 g per litre of water | Repeat after 15 days; the first spray on the first dry, calm morning | NRCP advisory 89 (copper hydroxide 2 g/l, sprays at 15-day intervals) [6]; APEDA / NRCP list (copper compounds 2–2.5 g/l) [9] |
| Preventive: neighbour warnings, the officer's advisories, routine sprays | Bordeaux mixture 1%, freshly prepared | 10 g copper sulphate + 10 g lime per litre | 15 days | NRCP advisory 89 (1% Bordeaux, freshly prepared) [6]; advisory 114 (1% Bordeaux on the evening after pruning) [8] |
| Alternative to copper hydroxide (not in the app yet) | Copper oxychloride 50% WP | 3 g per litre [6], or 2–2.5 g per litre [9] | 15 days | As above |

chunks.heading: The table
chunks.text: Removed: Streptocycline (streptomycin sulphate 90% + tetracycline hydrochloride 10%), which the table used to combine with copper oxychloride for curative sprays.

chunks.heading: Why the antibiotic is gone
chunks.text:
1. Regulation. The Union Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare issued the draft Prohibition of Streptomycin + Tetracycline in agriculture Order, 2021 on 17 December 2021 (listed as S.O. 5295(E)) [1, 2]. It would end the manufacture, import and formulation of the two antibiotics for agriculture from 1 February 2022 and ban their use in agriculture completely from 1 January 2024, coming into force on final publication in the Gazette [1]. It followed the Registration Committee's 2020 recommendation to phase them out [4]. A September 2022 report says the Central Insecticides Board discussed the ban and asked ICAR for more data [3]. We did not find the final gazetted order, so the legal status today is not confirmed. ICAR-NRCP's own researchers, writing in December 2024, cite the draft and describe the ban on use as taking effect from 1 January 2024 [5], while a 2025 field study still tested copper with Streptocycline [10].
2. Resistance. The same NRCP paper reports antibiotic resistance, and reduced sensitivity to antibiotics and copper, in field populations of the blight bacterium in India [5].
3. Public health. Streptomycin is a tuberculosis drug; antimicrobial resistance is the stated reason for the ban [1, 4].

chunks.heading: Why the antibiotic is gone
chunks.text: Whatever the final legal position, the policy direction and the national pomegranate centre both point away from antibiotics, so the app should not recommend one. To close this out, check the Gazette of India (egazette.gov.in) and the Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine and Storage for the final order, and record its number and date here.

chunks.heading: What is not handled yet
chunks.text:
- Pre-harvest interval. The APEDA list gives copper compounds a 60-day pre-harvest interval for pomegranate grown for export [9]. A curative copper spray in October conflicts with a November export harvest. Each lot passport now checks this: it flags any copper spray within 60 days before the picking and gives the first date a picking would clear it. The spray advice itself does not yet plan around the interval (roadmap item 2.5); until it does, the advice is for the domestic market and the label governs.
- Bronopol. According to the search index, NRCP's 2020 advisory 63 listed bronopol (2-bromo-2-nitropropane-1,3-diol 95%) at 5 g per 10 litres, with copper oxychloride or copper hydroxide and a sticker, as the alternative to Streptocycline [7]. We could not open that PDF to confirm it, and we have not checked bronopol's registration for pomegranate. It stays out of the app until an agronomist confirms the product, dose and label claim.
- Biological control. NRCP field trials of native Bacillus endophytes reduced blight by 47–68% over two seasons [5]. That is promising, but it is not yet a product recommendation.
- The community schedule. NRCP advises a six-step schedule, starting with the main pruning soon after harvest and including a 10% Bordeaux paste, that works only when all the orchards in a locality with blight follow it at the same time [6]. That fits the officer's advisories and the village goals, and belongs in the roadmap.
- Copper limits. Copper sprays can be phytotoxic above label rates, and the bacterium is showing reduced sensitivity to copper [5]. Keep to label doses and intervals; do not add sprays beyond the schedule.

chunks.heading: Models
chunks.text: Everything below runs in the browser from web/src/lib. Parameters are demo calibrations chosen to give a plausible season. They are not fitted to field data yet; the pilot (see ROADMAP.md) is where they get fitted and validated.

chunks.heading: 1. Weather
chunks.text:
Each season day has rain, temperature range, mean humidity, maximum wind and dominant direction, ET0, and leaf-wet hours:

| Days | Source | observed | live |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 June to yesterday | Open-Meteo archive (reanalysis), wet hours from its hourly series | yes | yes |
| Today to +6 days | Open-Meteo forecast, wet hours from the hourly forecast | no | yes |
| Beyond | Seeded synthetic climatology for the Phaltan rain shadow (monthly normals, wet-spell persistence) | no | no |

In 2026 the recorded canopy was wet about 11 hours a day from July to September and under an hour a day in October; 579 mm of rain fell from 1 June to 19 October.

chunks.heading: Favourability
chunks.text: On simulated days without hourly data the wet-canopy term falls back to $\text{clamp}\big((\overline{RH}d - 58)/27\big)$.

chunks.heading: Infection hazard
chunks.text:
For a healthy plot $p$ on day $d$, with neighbours $q$ within 6 km at distance $k{pq}$ and bearing $\beta{pq}$, and the day's wind blowing towards $\thetad$:

Six seed infections arrive between days 46 and 79 (mid-July to mid-August). Random draws are hashed per (plot, day, salt), so changing one plot never reshuffles another.

chunks.heading: Detection, advice, sprays
chunks.text:
- A symptomatic plot is found each day with probability 0.28 if the farmer uses the app (her own scan) and 0.06 otherwise (an officer's visit, stamped verified).
- A confirmed scan books a curative spray on the first sprayable day: rain under 1 mm, rain chance under 45%, wind under 15 km/h, maximum under 36 °C. Up to eight app-using neighbours within 2.5 km are warned, and 75% of them book a preventive spray for the same morning.
- A spray on a day with 5 mm of rain or more is washed off and repeated.

chunks.heading: Pest Radar (what the desk knows)
chunks.text: Built only from reported scans, never from the hidden infection state. For each H3 cell, scans in the last 14 days count with freshness $1 - \text{age}/14$; neighbouring cells add $0.3 + 0.35\cdot\text{align}$ of theirs; the sum is scaled by $0.6 + 0.6 fd$. Levels: watch ≥ 0.16, warning ≥ 0.55, outbreak ≥ 1.2.

chunks.heading: Calibration check: the same engine on recorded and synthetic weather
chunks.text:
| By 20 October 2026 | Synthetic weather | Recorded 2026 weather |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plots ever infected | 91 of 192 | 65 of 192 |
| Blight scans reported over the whole months of Jul / Aug / Sep / Oct | 10 / 31 / 23 / 20 | 3 / 18 / 22 / 18 |
| Cells on warning or outbreak at end of September | 16 | 12 |
| Washed-off spray (hero) | 27 Sep, 14 mm scripted | 21 Sep, 24 mm recorded |

The recorded season is drier than the climatology (mean RH 73 to 77% against 79 to 82%), and October was almost rainless, so spread stalls in October. That is what the screens now show.

chunks.heading: 3. Spread forecast (72 hours)
chunks.text:
src/lib/spread.ts. A forecast of where reported blight can travel in the next 72 hours, from the stamped hour.

Frames. 72 hourly frames with wind $(u, v)$ in km/h towards east and north at nine grid points, plus mean rain, humidity and temperature. When the clock is inside the live forecast, frames come from /api/weather/wind, nine Open-Meteo points over the taluka's bounding box, and wind at any location is bilinear between them. For any other hour, frames are built from that day's recorded (or simulated) daily weather: humidity peaks at dawn, temperature mid-afternoon, rain falls 15:00 to 20:00, and one wind (0.6 of the daily maximum) blows over the taluka. A demo rain input is laid over the first six hours of its day with a gust front of at least 14 km/h.

Hourly favourability.

chunks.heading: 3. Spread forecast (72 hours)
chunks.text:
Kernel. For each source cell $s$ (reported level $Ls$: watch, warning, outbreak, weights 0.5, 1.2, 2) and each hour, the wind at $s$ has speed $U$ and unit direction $\hat{u}$. A target cell at displacement $\vec{d}$ (km) has along-wind distance $x = \vec{d}\cdot\hat u$ and cross-wind distance $y$:

Exposure tiers: low ≥ 0.35, moderate ≥ 1.2, high ≥ 4. The desk shows exposure accumulated up to the scrubbed hour, each cell's peak hour, and the cells to warn (moderate or high, not already on warning).

chunks.heading: 3. Spread forecast (72 hours)
chunks.text:
Closing the loop. Warn adds { day, hexes } to overrides.advisories. In the engine, every plot in those cells that is not already symptomatic gets the advisory; app users book a preventive spray on the first sprayable day, and SMS recipients do so with probability 0.45. The ripple reports plots told, sprays booked, and the change in new infections over three weeks. On 19 September with the recorded weather: 62 plots told, 52 sprays booked, new infections 14 → 11.

Leaf wetness after rain. A canopy stays wet after rain stops, longer after heavy rain: after an hour with $P$ mm, the wet-canopy term ($0.45\,wT$) holds for $\min(10, \max(4, 3 + P))$ hours at that source, and two hours more in low-lying cells: the 28 cells at least 12 m below the mean of their neighbours (Copernicus DEM via Open-Meteo), where dew and cold air pool at night.

chunks.heading: 3. Spread forecast (72 hours)
chunks.text:
Does it work? The backtest. npm run backtest forecasts every cell with no blight reported, every day from 11 July to 25 September on the recorded weather, and asks whether blight is reported there 8 to 24 days later (an infection carried in the next 72 hours shows symptoms after a 10 to 14 day latent period, and is then scanned; a window of days 1 to 14 mostly scores infections that were already latent).

| 16,361 cell-days, 575 with new blight | ROC AUC |
| --- | --- |
| Spread forecast (reported cells, recorded weather) | 0.577 |
| Distance to the nearest reported cell | 0.559 |
| Oracle: the same forecast fed every symptomatic orchard, reported or not | 0.643 |

chunks.heading: 3. Spread forecast (72 hours)
chunks.text: The forecast's warn cells report blight later at 5.1% against a 3.5% base rate (1.46×) and catch 23.5% of new outbreaks; in September, the wettest month with the most reports, its AUC is 0.606 against 0.529. The oracle shows where the rest of the skill is: in reports. With every symptomatic orchard reported, the same forecast gains 0.07 AUC. The reports here are the simulation's own, so this tests the method and the harness; the pilot runs the same harness on real scans.

chunks.heading: 3. Spread forecast (72 hours)
chunks.text: Uncertainty: the ensemble. /api/weather/ensemble serves the 51 members (control + 50) of the ECMWF IFS 0.25° ensemble at Phaltan, hourly for four days. Each member becomes its own frames (its rain, humidity and wind, one wind for the taluka; demo rain stays in every member), the kernel runs once per member, six members per tick so the desk stays responsive, and the desk shows the share of members in which each cell reaches moderate exposure, plus the 10th to 90th percentile of rain per hour. On 20 October 2026 all 51 members kept Phaltan dry for four days.

chunks.heading: 3. Spread forecast (72 hours)
chunks.text:
Storm brush. The officer draws a track; it becomes a rain cell (8 mm an hour at the core, Gaussian with a 4 km radius) moving along the track at about 12 km/h (3 to 8 hours). Rain at each source is summed over the hour in quarter-hour steps as the cell passes, and within the cell the wind becomes a gust front of at least 22 km/h along the track. It is a what-if: the warn button is disabled while a drawn storm is on the map.

What it is not. It is not fitted. Rain splash and wind-driven rain carry Xanthomonas over short distances; the reach and widths above are plausible placeholders. Validation plan: compare forecast exposure with the cells where scans are reported in the following 14 days during the pilot, and fit $R$, $\sigma$ and the weights by maximum likelihood.

chunks.heading: 4. Water Commons
chunks.text:
Every three days from bahar + 20 days, each plot needs

with $Kc$ from 0.3 (rest) to 0.9 (fruit development). Irrigation is skipped after 10 mm of rain; when 5 mm or more is forecast for tomorrow, app users skip and the litres count as kept in the ground. The village goal is 80% of plots following forecast irrigation.

chunks.heading: 5. Harvest Wave and markets
chunks.text:
- Four pickings at harvest start + 0, 8, 16, 25 days, sharing 20, 35, 30 and 15% of the expected crop (about 20 kg a crate). Rain of 8 mm or more on or after a picking day brings it a day earlier to avoid cracking.
- Grade follows infection at harvest start: never infected A, treated B (88% of the crop), symptomatic C (60%). Grade price factors 1, 0.68, 0.42.
- Prices by market and day: a monthly base, an AR(1) noise, and pressure from arrivals, $\text{price} \propto \text{clamp}\big(1 - 0.42(a/\bar a - 1)\big)$, with a seasonal hump in arrivals and a Pune glut around 17 November. Grade A lots go to the market with the best net after freight and commission.

chunks.heading: 6. Pooled runs
chunks.text: Bookings are grouped by day, village collection point and market and packed largest-first into 75-crate vehicles, splitting a lot across vehicles when needed. Runs to Phaltan leave at 05:15, to Pune at 01:30 and to Vashi at 21:00. Routes follow the real road graph from each collection point (Dijkstra in build-geo.ts).

chunks.heading: 7. Scan Lens (on device)
chunks.text:
- MobileNetV2, PlantVillage, 38 classes, fp32 ONNX in ONNX Runtime Web (wasm, single thread), in a module worker. 224 × 224, ImageNet normalisation.
- Crop-conditioned: the farmer picks the crop, the softmax is renormalised over that crop's classes, and the unconditioned first guess is shown when it disagrees.
- Where it looked: a 7 × 7 occlusion map, batched, drawn as a red heat overlay.
- Honest numbers: 95.4% on PlantVillage lab photos (model card); on three public field photos it misread two diseases. Pomegranate has no class in PlantVillage, so the pomegranate result is scripted until ml/train.py is run on Phaltan photos.

chunks.heading: 7. Scan Lens (on device)
chunks.text: Photo check. Before inference, a 192 px grey copy of the photo gives sharpness (variance of the Laplacian) and light (mean brightness). On the sample leaves, sharp photos scored 230 to 5,900 and a 1.5 px blur 10 to 36, so under 60 is blurry; under 65 brightness is too dark, over 215 washed out. The camera view runs the same check twice a second and turns its frame violet when the photo will read.

chunks.heading: 8. Sale slip check
chunks.text: Languages. English is read first; if fewer than four of the key fields come out, the photo is read again with Tesseract's Marathi and English models together (2 MB more, loaded on demand). Devanagari digits become ASCII, zero-width joiners are removed, gaps inside numbers close up, and a final separator with one or two digits is the only decimal mark (OCR reads Indian commas as points). Labels are matched in both languages (अडत, हमाली, तोलाई, मोटार भाडे, एकूण वजावट, निव्वळ देय).

chunks.heading: 8. Sale slip check
chunks.text: Corrections, only when a line proves itself. A number is corrected only if (a) its own line says what it must be: a multiplication on the label ("हमाली 63 x 5" must be 315), a percentage of the gross ("Adat 6%"), or weight × rate for the gross; and (b) it was read with under 90% confidence and is one digit away, or read under 50% and cannot be trusted at all. With exactly one weak line and a clearly read total, the total less the other lines gives that line, if the digits read agree. Totals and the net are never corrected: that is where a real overcharge would hide. A total one digit from the lines, read unclearly, is shown as check the total, not counted as money owed. A number with stray characters stuck to it is left blank for the farmer; nothing is guessed. Every correction is listed and underlined in violet.

chunks.heading: 8. Sale slip check
chunks.text: Checks: weight against crates × 20 kg (flag below 95%); gross = weight × rate; each charge against the rate card (commission 6% of gross, hamali ₹5 and weighment ₹1 a crate, freight the run's rate a crate); any charge not on the card; deductions add up to the total; gross less total equals net. The rate is compared with the day's modal price for the grade (information only). Numbers read with under 75% confidence are underlined for the farmer to check.

chunks.heading: 9. Lot passport and the export check
chunks.text: src/lib/lot.ts builds one passport per picking (TAR-214-P1): village and H3 cell (never the gat number or full name), picking date, crates and grade, run and market, every spray and scan before picking, drip water and water skipped. The export check flags any copper spray (every product in the table is copper-based) within 60 days before picking, the interval the APEDA list gives for copper on pomegranate, and gives the first date a picking would clear it. It is not a certificate: registration and residue testing go through APEDA's AnarNet.

chunks.heading: 10. Voice
chunks.text: Intent by keyword in Marathi and English (spray failure, next spray, irrigation, harvest date, market, sale, blight nearby), answered by builders that quote the record with dates and amounts, with sources and sure chips. Unknown intents go to the officer with the plot's last five entries. Speech in and out through the Web Speech API (mr-IN).

chunks.heading: Where
chunks.text:
Phaltan taluka, Satara district, western Maharashtra. It sits in the rain shadow east of the Sahyadri: the season's rain is modest and patchy, so most orchards run on drip irrigation from wells and the Nira canals. The recorded season so far (1 June to 19 October 2026, Open-Meteo archive at Phaltan) brought 579 mm: 131 mm in June, 269 mm in July, 86 mm in August, 91 mm in September and 2 mm in October.

The hero crop is pomegranate (mostly the Bhagwa variety). Growers force flowering by withholding water and pruning, a practice called taking a bahar: Ambia bahar flowers in January and February, Mrig bahar in June and July, Hasta bahar in September and October. KhetKundli follows a Mrig bahar season: bahar in June, fruit through the monsoon, pickings from November into January.

chunks.heading: Who
chunks.text:
| Person | Job to be done | Today |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The farmer (our persona: Sunita Jadhav, gat 214, Taradgaon, 1.5 acres on drip) | Catch blight early, spray when it will stick, irrigate only when needed, pick and sell at the right time and place, get paid what was agreed | Advice is generic and in English; her own history lives in her memory and a notebook; she cannot see her neighbours' orchards |
| The extension officer / KVK | Know where disease is moving and warn the right farmers before it arrives; answer questions | Hears about outbreaks late, by phone; too many farmers to visit |
| The FPO coordinator | Plan transport and market for many small lots; negotiate fair deductions | Pickings and lot sizes are known only on the morning; transport is booked plot by plot |

chunks.heading: Six problems that are really one
chunks.text:
1. Bacterial blight spreads unseen. Bacterial blight (telya, caused by Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. punicae) is the most feared disease of pomegranate in Maharashtra. It moves between orchards in wind-driven rain splash and on wet canopies, and through tools and cuttings. Once established in an orchard it is very hard to clear, so the value lies in warning the next orchard before it is infected. No single farmer can see a front that crosses village boundaries.
2. Sprays are wasted. A copper spray needs a few dry hours to set. A spray at three in the afternoon before evening rain is money and chemical washed into the soil; the farmer often does not know why it failed.
3. Water is shared but used alone. Irrigation decisions ignore the forecast: a plot is watered the day before 10 mm of rain, and the aquifer that the whole village draws on pays for it.
4. Everyone picks the same week. Crop stage decides harvest timing, so a village's orchards come due together, Pune and Vashi markets glut, and prices fall exactly when most fruit arrives.
5. Transport is booked lot by lot. Small lots (20 to 100 crates) travel in half-empty vehicles because nobody knows the neighbour's picking date three days ahead.
6. The sale slip is not checked. The commission agent's patti lists gross, commission, hamali, weighment and freight. Few farmers check the arithmetic or compare the charges with what was agreed.

chunks.heading: Six problems that are really one
chunks.text: The common cause is that each plot's information is trapped in that plot, while the decisions that matter (warn, spray, irrigate, pick, pool, check) depend on many plots and on the weather together.

chunks.heading: The idea
chunks.text:
Give every plot a season record (its kundli) that every feature writes to and reads from. Then read the records together:

The key claim: the crop-advisory layer is the demand forecast for the logistics layer, because crop stage on every plot predicts when each village will pick. And the disease layer is only as good as the reports flowing into it, which is why the farmer's phone has to be worth opening every day.

chunks.text:
| Source | Problem statement | KhetKundli module | Where |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Govt. of Punjab | Smart crop advisory for small and marginal farmers | Advice from the plot's own record and the live forecast | Phone: today slip, spray window |
| Govt. of Kerala | AI-powered personal farming assistant | The kundli wheel: one plot, one season, remembered | Phone: wheel, record |

chunks.heading: Principles
chunks.text:
1. One record, many faces. Nothing stands alone; every feature reads and writes the record.
2. Collective sight is the point. Show what only many plots together reveal.
3. Prove, don't claim. Real weather, real map, on-device models; everything simulated is labelled.
4. Doses never come from a model. Spray products and doses come from a fixed rules table that agronomists must verify.
5. The farmer's data stays hers. Shared maps aggregate to roughly 5 km² cells; photos and slips are read on the phone and are not uploaded.
6. Marathi first where the farmer is. Every farmer-facing line has a Marathi twin; voice works in Marathi.

chunks.heading: Glossary
chunks.text:
| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Adat, adatya (अडत, अडत्या) | Commission; the commission agent who auctions the farmer's lot at the APMC and pays the farmer after deductions |
| APMC | Agricultural Produce Market Committee: the regulated market yard (Phaltan APMC; Pune market yard; Vashi APMC in Navi Mumbai) |
| Bahar (बहार) | Forced flowering in pomegranate by withholding water and pruning. Ambia bahar flowers in Jan–Feb, Mrig in Jun–Jul, Hasta in Sep–Oct |
| Bhagwa | The main pomegranate variety grown in the area (saffron-red arils) |
| Crate | The unit for pickings and transport; the engine uses about 20 kg a crate |
| ET0 | Reference evapotranspiration (mm/day): how much water a reference crop would use today, from the weather. Multiplied by a crop coefficient Kc for the stage |
| FPO | Farmer Producer Organisation: a farmers' company that aggregates produce and negotiates with agents and buyers |
| Gat number (गट क्रमांक) | The land-record survey number that identifies a plot in the village |
| H3 | A global grid of hexagons. KhetKundli uses resolution 7 (cells of about 5 km²) so that shared maps never show a single farm |
| Hamali (हमाली) | Loading and unloading charge, per crate |
| Kundli (कुंडली) | A birth chart. Here, the plot's season record that keeps updating |
| KVK | Krishi Vigyan Kendra: the district farm science centre that runs extension work |
| Leaf-wet hours | Hours in a day when the canopy is wet (rain, or relative humidity at or above 85%) at 18 to 35 °C: the weather in which bacterial blight moves |
| Modal price | The most common auction price on a day at a market, as published by Agmarknet |
| Motor bhada (मोटार भाडे) | Freight |
| Patti (पट्टी) | The sale slip the agent gives the farmer: lot, weight, rate, gross, deductions, net |
| PHI | Pre-harvest interval: the minimum days between a spray and picking, from the product label |
| Pooled run | One vehicle carrying several farmers' crates from a village collection point to the market |
| Rate card | The deductions the FPO agreed with an agent for pooled lots: commission %, hamali and weighment per crate, freight per crate |
| Ripple | What KhetKundli shows when an event changes the season: the list of consequences across modules |
| Telya (तेल्या) | Bacterial blight of pomegranate, Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. punicae; named for the oily spots on leaves and fruit |
| Tolai (तोलाई) | Weighment charge |
| Override | An event that changes the simulated season: a scan, a rain forecast, a picking date, an advisory, a sale slip |

chunks.heading: How a screen says where a number comes from
chunks.text: Each figure carries a rubber stamp: Live (forecast or on-device now), Recorded (real past data) or Simulated. The forecast panel's stamp follows its frames (live grid, recorded day, simulated day); the weather slip follows the first day shown. Synthetic plot records say so in their headers and footers.

chunks.heading: Privacy
chunks.text:
- Shared maps aggregate. The desk shows H3 resolution-7 cells (about 5 km²) and approximate village areas; individual farms are not drawn on shared views. The plot record view is for the farmer and the officer she asks.
- Photos stay on the phone. Leaf scans and slip photos are processed in the browser; only the result (a finding with a confidence, or the slip's numbers) enters the record.
- No personal data in URLs. Sync messages travel in POST bodies and server-sent events.
- For the pilot, the roadmap adds phone-number accounts with explicit, purpose-bound consent under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023: consent to share the plot's reported scans with the FPO for Pest Radar, separate consent for market data, the right to see and erase one's record, and data held by the FPO as the farmers' own organisation.

chunks.heading: Caveats
chunks.text:
- The archive is a reanalysis grid of several kilometres, not a station in the orchard; local showers can be missed or smeared.
- The wind grid has nine points across a taluka roughly 60 km wide; valleys and hills are not resolved.
- Agmarknet prices are what markets report; arrivals and modal prices can be revised.
- OCR reads printed English labels and Western digits; Marathi labels and handwriting need the work listed in the roadmap.

chunks.heading: Roadmap
chunks.text: From a demo that runs on real weather to a record that real farmers keep. Each item says what the farmer or officer gets, how it works, what data it needs, and when it is done. Dates are plans; partners named below are organisations we intend to approach, not agreements. Targets are hypotheses to test, not results.

chunks.heading: Where we are (20 October 2026)
chunks.text: Built and tested: the kundli wheel, today slip and spray window; Scan Lens on the device; Marathi voice answers from the record with escalation to an officer; the sale slip check with on-device OCR; the taluka desk with Pest Radar, Harvest Wave, Water Commons and pooled runs; the season engine running on recorded 2026 weather; a live wind field and 72-hour spread forecast with one-tap advisories by app or SMS, run on all 51 ECMWF ensemble members for a chance by cell; the storm brush what-if; lot passports with QR codes and an export pre-harvest check; the neighbour pulse on the phone; a photo check before scans; officer replies read aloud; offline-first sync (an IndexedDB outbox ordered by hybrid logical clocks, an idempotent relay with last-writer-wins); Marathi slip reading with self-proving corrections; contour lines from real elevation and low-lying wetness; a forecast backtest; the season share card; the pitch. Simulated: the farmers and their plots, mandi prices without a key, the specimen slips.

chunks.heading: H1 · Pilot: one FPO, three villages, the Ambia bahar of 2027
chunks.text: Goal: about 150 farmers keep their record for a full season, the officer uses the desk weekly, and every model gets its first field numbers.

chunks.heading: 1.1 Accounts, consent and a real record store
chunks.text:
Farmer gets: her record survives a lost phone; she decides who sees what. Officer gets: the real taluka, not a simulation.

- Identity: phone-number accounts (OTP), one farmer to many plots, plots registered by gat number and a GPS walk of the boundary (or chosen from the village map with the farmer).
- Consent (Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023): purpose-bound, revocable consents stored as events: share reported scans with my FPO for Pest Radar, share pickings for pooled runs, share sale slips anonymously for the fair-slip index. A record export and an erase request in the app.
- Store: Postgres 16 with PostGIS and the h3 extension. Append-only plotevents; projections as materialised views; the browser engine stays as the simulator and the "what if".

- Corrections are new events that point at the old one, so the record keeps its history and its inks.

chunks.heading: 1.1 Accounts, consent and a real record store
chunks.text: Done when: a farmer can reinstall the app and see her season; the desk reads only consented events.

chunks.heading: 1.2 Offline-first sync
chunks.text: Built in October 2026 (phone side and relay): durable messages are stamped with a hybrid logical clock and kept in an IndexedDB outbox until the relay accepts them; the relay ignores stamps it has seen and keeps the newest overrides by clock, so a phone reconnecting with older changes cannot overwrite newer ones; the phone header shows Synced, Sending or Offline · N to send. Still to do for the pilot: the server-side event store below, and SMS.

chunks.heading: 1.2 Offline-first sync
chunks.text:
- The phone keeps an outbox of events in IndexedDB; each event has a UUIDv7 and a hybrid logical clock. Upload is idempotent (the server ignores ids it has seen); download is by cursor. Because events are append-only, there are no merge conflicts to resolve.
- Background Sync where the browser supports it; otherwise retry on open.
- SMS fallback for the events that cannot wait: a blight scan is packed into one 160-character message (plot, day, finding, confidence) to an SMS gateway number.
- Live updates over a hosted WebSocket channel replace the demo relay.

Done when: a week offline syncs in one go with no duplicates, and a scan in a no-data area reaches the desk by SMS.

chunks.heading: 1.3 Scan Lens v2: pomegranate, on the NPU
chunks.text:
- Classes start with what matters most: bacterial blight on leaf and fruit, healthy leaf and fruit, and "something else, ask the officer"; fungal fruit spots (Cercospora, Alternaria, anthracnose) follow as data allows.
- Report per-class recall on a held-out village, not overall accuracy on random splits.
- A curative recommendation needs a confident scan or the officer's confirmation; below the floor, the farmer is asked to retake or send to the officer.
- Image quality check before inference: blur (variance of the Laplacian), exposure and leaf coverage, with on-screen guidance.

Done when: blight recall on the held-out village is published, with the confusion matrix, in the app's model card.

chunks.heading: 1.4 Marathi voice v2, WhatsApp and IVR
chunks.text:
- Speech: Marathi ASR from open Indic models (AI4Bharat IndicConformer) or the Bhashini APIs, with on-device Web Speech as the offline fallback; Marathi TTS for answers.
- Understanding: a small multilingual intent classifier (IndicBERT or MuRIL) trained on the pilot's real questions; answers still built from the record by code.
- Language models only rephrase an answer the code has already built, and draft replies for the officer to edit; never doses, never facts that are not in the record or the rules table.
- Channels: WhatsApp Business messages for advisories and replies (voice notes in Marathi); a missed-call IVR that calls back with today's action, for farmers without a smartphone. The spread forecast's by SMS path becomes real here.

Done when: farmers without smartphones receive the same advisories, and the Ask log shows the intents the classifier gets wrong.

chunks.heading: 1.5 Real pattis and the FPO's rate card
chunks.text:
- Collect slips from the pilot farmers (names blurred) to tune the parser to each agent's layout.
- Built in October 2026: Tesseract's Marathi model loads on demand when English reads noise; Devanagari digits and Marathi labels are parsed; a misread is corrected only when its own line proves it (a multiplication on the label, a percentage of the gross, or the one weak line under a clearly read total), unreadable numbers are left blank, and a total or net is never corrected. Next: a table-layout pass for column slips, and a handwritten-digit model (Devanagari and Western) for hand-written amounts.
- The rate card becomes data: the FPO records what it agreed with each agent, per market and season; the slip check compares against that.
- Fair-slip index (anonymous, aggregated): share of slips with charges above the card, per market, for the FPO's negotiations; no agent is named on farmer screens.

chunks.heading: 1.6 Live mandi prices
chunks.text: Agmarknet daily modal prices and arrivals for pomegranate at Phaltan, Pune, Vashi and Solapur through the data.gov.in API; the slip check's rate comparison and the market ledger become live.

chunks.heading: 1.7 Spread forecast v2
chunks.text:
- Uncertainty (built in October 2026): the forecast runs on each of the 51 ECMWF ensemble members at Phaltan, and the desk shows the share of members in which each cell reaches moderate exposure, with the 10–90% range of rain in the hour strip. Next: per-member wind fields at the nine grid points rather than one wind per member.
- Fit the kernel: the scoring harness is built (npm run backtest): over the recorded season the forecast scores ROC AUC 0.577 against 0.559 for distance alone and 0.643 for an oracle that sees every symptomatic orchard, scored on reports 8 to 24 days later to allow for the latent period. During the pilot, run it on real reports and fit reach $R$, width $\sigma$ and source weights by maximum likelihood.
- Second channel: pruning gangs and shared sprayers carry bacteria between orchards; let farmers log who worked in the orchard and add that contact network to the forecast.
- Terrain: built in part: real elevation (Copernicus DEM via Open-Meteo) draws the survey sheet's contours and marks 28 low-lying cells where dew holds two hours longer. Next: slope and aspect, and wind channelled along the valleys.

chunks.heading: 1.7 Spread forecast v2
chunks.text:
Done when: the forecast beats the distance-only baseline on the pilot's detections, or we say plainly that it does not.

---

chunks.heading: 2.1 Plot health from Sentinel-2
chunks.text:
- Sentinel-2 L2A (10 m, about every 5 days) from the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (STAC search plus openEO or the Process API). NDVI and NDRE per plot polygon, with clouds and shadows removed using the scene classification layer.
- Sentinel-1 radar backscatter fills the monsoon gaps when clouds hide the optical images.
- Anomaly: compare each plot with plots of the same village and bahar stage; flag a canopy falling behind for a scan or a visit.
- On the phone: a thin greenness ring on the kundli wheel, one tick per clear image.

chunks.heading: 2.2 Water Commons v2: the aquifer as a passbook
chunks.text:
- Groundwater levels from GSDA and CGWB observation wells (India-WRIS), plus farmer-reported well depths (a photo of a marked rope, monthly).
- A village water budget: recharge from recorded rain, withdrawals from the irrigation the records imply (ET0 × Kc), shown as a passbook with deposits and withdrawals.
- Flow meters on a sample of drip systems to verify that "skipped before rain" saves what the model says.

chunks.heading: 2.3 Harvest and price forecasting
chunks.text:
- Picking dates: a gradient-boosted model on bahar date, growing degree days from recorded temperature, canopy greenness and the pilot's actual pickings, with prediction intervals.
- Prices and gluts: Agmarknet arrivals and modal prices for pomegranate at the main terminal markets, plus our own forecast of arrivals from the taluka, festival calendar and weather; LightGBM quantile models (or a temporal fusion transformer if the data supports it), compared against a seasonal naive baseline.
- On the phone: If you pick on 12 November and sell in Pune, expect ₹x to ₹y a kg, with the uncertainty shown.

chunks.heading: 2.4 Pooled runs, optimised
chunks.text:
- Capacitated vehicle routing with time windows (OR-Tools): collection points as pickups, market opening as the deadline, real vehicles with capacity and cost per km; re-solved each evening from the next day's bookings.
- A driver app: route, pickups, crate counts with a photo at each stop, GPS trace; cost split per crate on the farmers' slips.
- Lot passport (built in October 2026): a QR per picking (cell, picking date, grade, sprays, water, run, export check) that the buyer can scan; next, sign the passport so a buyer can trust it was not edited.

chunks.heading: 2.5 Export-ready record
chunks.text:
The first piece is built: each lot passport checks copper sprays against the 60-day pre-harvest interval from the APEDA list and says when a picking would clear it.

Pomegranate exports to the EU go through APEDA's AnarNet traceability system. The record already holds every spray with product and date; add each product's label pre-harvest interval and residue limits, check them against the planned picking date, schedule residue tests, and produce the plot's spray dossier for registration.

chunks.heading: 2.6 The officer's console
chunks.text:
Accounts and roles for officers and FPO staff; field visit planning from the inbox and the radar (shortest route through today's visits); cohort views of adoption and outcomes; the fair-slip index.

---

chunks.heading: H3 · Platform (2028 onward)
chunks.text:
- More talukas: the pomegranate belts of Solapur, Sangli and Ahmednagar districts share the crop, the disease and the markets.
- More crops: grapes, onion and sugarcane in Phaltan itself; the record, the radar and the wave are crop-agnostic, the models are not.
- Public systems, with consent: link to AgriStack Farmer ID and the digital crop survey where available; ONDC for direct sales.
- Open data: an API of aggregated, delayed, k-anonymous cell-level disease and harvest data for researchers and the agriculture department.
- Federated learning for Scan Lens: improve the model from phones without moving photos.

---

chunks.heading: How we will know it works
chunks.text:
| Question | Measure | Target for the pilot (hypothesis) | How measured |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Do farmers keep the record? | Weekly active farmers | 60% of enrolled | Event log |
| Does the radar see enough? | Plots with a scan in the last 14 days during the monsoon | 50% | Event log |
| Are sprays wasted less? | Sprays followed by 5 mm of rain within 6 hours | Half of the pre-pilot baseline | Records against recorded weather; baseline survey |
| Does the forecast warn the right plots? | ROC AUC of 72-hour exposure for detections in the next 14 days | Above the distance-only baseline | Pilot detections |
| Do advisories reach people in time? | Plots in the plume reached within 2 hours, by any channel | 80% | Delivery receipts |
| Is water kept? | Litres skipped before rain on metered plots | Within 20% of the model's estimate | Flow meters |
| Are slips fair? | Slips flagged; rupees recovered after a dispute | Measured, not targeted | Slip checks, follow-up |
| Do runs fill? | Average fill of pooled runs | 80% | Run records |

chunks.heading: Risks
chunks.text:
| Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- |
| Too few scans make the radar blind | Officer visits recorded as verified scans; Neighbour pulse to reward reporting; SMS reporting |
| A wrong diagnosis leads to a wrong spray | Confidence floor; officer confirmation for curative advice; doses only from the reviewed table |
| Spray advice falls out of date or breaks a regulation | Table owned by a named agronomist, reviewed each season against current approvals |
| Agents push back on slip checks | Compare against the FPO's own agreed card; aggregate index only; the farmer decides whether to dispute |
| Connectivity in orchards | Offline-first, SMS for urgent events, IVR |
| Low-end phones | Test on 2 GB RAM Android; models under 10 MB; OCR only on demand |
| Privacy and trust | Consent per purpose, cell-level maps, photos on the device, FPO as data steward |
| The model's licence or data rights | Train our own pomegranate model on consented photos; publish its card |

chunks.heading: What we need
chunks.text:
- Agronomy: a plant pathologist to review the spray table and label photos (ICAR-NRCP Solapur, MPKV Rahuri or KVK staff, to be approached).
- A pilot FPO in Phaltan taluka willing to share rate cards and run the desk weekly.
- Field time: photo collection days in blight season; slip collection after pickings.
- Devices: three low-end Android phones for testing; flow meters for a sample of plots.
- Keys and services: a data.gov.in API key; an SMS gateway and WhatsApp Business account; hosting for Postgres and the realtime channel.
